In 2005, it was revealed that the implementation of copy protection measures on about 22 million CDs distributed by Sony BMG installed one of two pieces of software that provided a form of digital rights management (DRM) by modifying the operating system to interfere with CD copying. Neither program could easily be uninstalled, and they created vulnerabilities that were exploited by unrelated malware. One of the programs would install and "phone home" with reports on the user's private listening habits, even if the user refused its end-user license agreement (EULA), while the other was not mentioned in the EULA at all. Both programs contained code from several pieces of copylefted free software in an apparent infringement of copyright, and configured the operating system to hide the software's existence, leading to both programs being classified as rootkits.

Sony BMG initially denied that the rootkits were harmful. It then released an official uninstaller for one of the programs that merely made the program's files visible while also installing additional software that could not be easily removed, collected an email address from the user and introduced further security vulnerabilities.

Following public outcry, government investigations and class-action lawsuits in 2005 and 2006, Sony BMG partially addressed the scandal with consumer settlements, a recall of about 10% of the affected CDs and the suspension of CD copy-protection efforts in early 2007.

In August 2000, statements by Sony Pictures Entertainment U.S. senior vice president Steve Heckler foreshadowed the events of late 2005. Heckler told attendees at the Americas Conference on Information Systems: "The industry will take whatever steps it needs to protect itself and protect its revenue streams ... It will not lose that revenue stream, no matter what ... Sony is going to take aggressive steps to stop this. We will develop technology that transcends the individual user. We will firewall Napster at source – we will block it at your cable company. We will block it at your phone company. We will block it at your ISP. We will firewall it at your PC ... These strategies are being aggressively pursued because there is simply too much at stake."[1]

In Europe, BMG created a minor scandal in 2001 when it released Natalie Imbruglia's second album White Lilies Island without warning labels stating that the CD contained copy protection.[2][3] The CDs were eventually replaced.[2][3] BMG and Sony both released copy-protected versions of certain releases in certain markets in late 2001,[4][5] and a late 2002 report indicated that all BMG CDs sold in Europe would contain some form of copy protection.[6]

Copy-protection software

[edit]

The two pieces of copy-protection software at issue in the 2005–2007 scandal were included on over 22 million CDs[7] marketed by Sony BMG, the record company formed by the 2004 merger of Sony and BMG's recorded music divisions. About two million of those CDs,[7] spanning 52 titles, contained First 4 Internet (F4I)'s Extended Copy Protection (XCP), which was installed on Microsoft Windows systems after the user accepted the EULA, which made no mention of the software. The remaining 20 million CDs,[7] spanning 50 titles,[8] contained SunnComm's MediaMax CD-3, which was installed on either Microsoft Windows or macOS systems after the user was presented with the EULA, regardless of whether the user accepted it. However, macOS prompted the user for confirmation when the software attempted to modify the OS, whereas Windows did not.

The scandal began on October 31, 2005, when Winternals researcher Mark Russinovich posted to his blog a detailed description and technical analysis of F4I's XCP software that he determined had been recently installed on his computer by a Sony BMG music CD. Russinovich compared the software to a rootkit because of its surreptitious installation and efforts to hide its existence. He noted that the EULA does not mention the software, and he charged that the software is illegitimate and that digital rights management had "gone too far".[9]

Anti-virus firm F-Secure concurred: "Although the software isn't directly malicious, the used rootkit hiding techniques are exactly the same used by malicious software to hide. The DRM software will cause many similar false alarms with all AV software that detect rootkits. ... Thus it is very inappropriate for commercial software to use these techniques."[10] After public pressure, Symantec[11] and other anti-virus vendors included detection for the rootkit in their products as well, and Microsoft announced that it would include detection and removal capabilities in its security patches.[12]

Russinovich discovered numerous problems with XCP:

  • It creates security holes that can be exploited by malicious software such as worms or viruses.
  • It constantly runs in the background and excessively consumes system resources, slowing down the user's computer, regardless of whether a protected CD is playing.
  • It employs unsafe procedures to start and stop, which could lead to system crashes.
  • It has no uninstaller, and is installed in such a way that inexpert attempts to uninstall it can cause the operating system to fail to recognize existing drives.

Soon after Russinovich's first post, several trojans and worms exploiting XCP's security holes appeared.[13] Some even used the vulnerabilities to cheat in online games.[14]

Sony BMG quickly released software to remove the rootkit component of XCP from affected Microsoft Windows computers,[15] but after Russinovich analyzed the utility, he reported in his blog that it only exacerbated the security problems and raised further concerns about privacy.[16] Russinovich noted that the removal program merely unmasked the hidden files installed by the rootkit but did not actually remove the rootkit. He also reported that it installed additional software that could not be uninstalled. In order to download the uninstaller, he found that it was necessary to provide an e-mail address (which the Sony BMG Privacy Policy implied was added to various bulk e-mail lists) and to install an ActiveX control containing backdoor methods (marked as "safe for scripting" and thus prone to exploits).[17] Microsoft later issued a killbit for the ActiveX control.

On November 18, 2005, Sony BMG provided a "new and improved" removal tool to remove the rootkit component of XCP from affected Microsoft Windows computers.[citation needed]

Legal and financial problems

[edit]

On November 15, 2005, vnunet.com announced[18] that Sony BMG was backing out of its copy-protection software, recalling unsold CDs from all stores and allowing consumers to exchange affected CDs for versions without the software. The Electronic Frontier Foundation compiled a partial list of CDs with XCP.[19] Sony BMG maintained that "there were no security risks associated with the anti-piracy technology" despite numerous virus and malware reports. On November 16, 2005, US-CERT, part of the United States Department of Homeland Security, issued an advisory on XCP DRM. It said that XCP uses rootkit technology to hide certain files from the user and that the technique is a security threat to users. They also said that one of the uninstallation options provided by Sony BMG introduces further vulnerabilities. US-CERT advised: "Do not install software from sources that you do not expect to contain software, such as an audio CD."[20]

Sony BMG announced that it had instructed retailers to remove any unsold music discs containing the software from their shelves.[21] Internet-security expert Dan Kaminsky estimated that XCP was in use on more than 500,000 networks.[22]

CDs with XCP technology can be identified by the letters "XCP" printed on the back cover of the jewel case for the CD according to SonyBMG's XCP FAQ.[23]

On November 16, 2005, Reuters reported that Sony BMG would exchange affected CDs for new unprotected discs.[24] As a part of the swap program, consumers could mail their XCP-protected CDs to Sony BMG and receive an unprotected disc via return mail.

On November 29, investigators for New York attorney general Eliot Spitzer found that, despite the recall of November 15, Sony BMG CDs with XCP were still for sale at some New York City music retail outlets. Spitzer said: "It is unacceptable that more than three weeks after this serious vulnerability was revealed, these same CDs are still on shelves, during the busiest shopping days of the year, [and] I strongly urge all retailers to heed the warnings issued about these products, pull them from distribution immediately, and ship them back to Sony."[25]

The next day, Massachusetts attorney general Tom Reilly announced that Sony BMG CDs with XCP were still available in Boston despite the Sony BMG recall of November 15.[26] He advised consumers not to purchase the Sony BMG CDs with XCP and said that he was conducting an investigation of Sony BMG.

Sony BMG's website offered US consumers a link to "Class Action Settlement Information Regarding XCP And MediaMax Content Protection"[27] with online claim filing and links to software updates and uninstallers. The deadline for submitting a claim was June 30, 2007. The website offered an explanation of the events as well as a list of all affected CDs.[28]

On November 21, 2005, Texas attorney general Greg Abbott sued Sony BMG.[29] The suit was the first filed by a U.S. state and was also the first filed under the state's 2005 spyware law. It alleged that the company surreptitiously installed the spyware on millions of CDs.

On December 21, 2005, Abbott added new allegations to the lawsuit,[30] claiming that MediaMax violated the state's spyware and deceptive trade practices laws because the MediaMax software would be installed on a computer even if the user declined the license agreement authorizing the action. Abbott stated: "We keep discovering additional methods Sony used to deceive Texas consumers who thought they were simply buying music", and "Thousands of Texans are now potential victims of this deceptive game Sony played with consumers for its own purposes." In addition to violations of the Consumer Protection Against Computer Spyware Act of 2005, which allowed for civil penalties of $100,000 for each violation of the law, the alleged violations added in the updated lawsuit carried maximum penalties of $20,000 per violation.[31][32] Sony was ordered to pay $750,000 in legal fees to Texas, accept customer returns of affected CDs, place a conspicuous detailed notice on its homepage, make "keyword buys" to alert consumers by advertising with Google, Yahoo! and MSN, pay up to $150 per damaged computer and agree to other remedies. Sony BMG also had to agree that it would not bring any claim that the legal settlement in any way constitutes the approval of the court.[33]

New York and California class-action suits

[edit]

Class-action suits were filed against Sony BMG in New York and California.[34]

On December 30, 2005, The New York Times reported that Sony BMG had reached a tentative settlement of the lawsuits, proposing two ways of compensating consumers who had purchased the affected CDs.[35]

In Italy, ALCEI [it] (an association similar to EFF) also reported the rootkit to the Financial Police, asking for an investigation under various computer crime allegations, along with a technical analysis of the rootkit.[36][37]

The U.S. Department of Justice made no comment on whether it would take any criminal action against Sony. However, Stewart Baker of the Department of Homeland Security publicly admonished Sony, stating, "it's your intellectual property—it's not your computer."[38]

On November 21, the EFF announced that it was also pursuing a lawsuit over both XCP and the SunnComm MediaMax DRM technology. The EFF lawsuit also involved issues concerning the Sony BMG end-user license agreement.

It was reported on December 24, 2005, that Florida attorney general Charlie Crist was investigating Sony BMG spyware.[39]

On January 30, 2007, the U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC) announced a settlement with Sony BMG on charges that the CD copy protection had violated federal law[40]—Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act, 15 USC 45(a)—by engaging in unfair and deceptive business practices.[41] The settlement required Sony BMG to reimburse consumers up to $150 to repair damage that resulted directly from its attempts to remove the software installed without their consent.[40] The settlement also required them to provide clear and prominent disclosure on the packaging of future CDs of any limits on copying or restrictions on the use of playback devices, and the company was prohibited from installing content-protection software without obtaining consumers' authorization.[40] FTC chairwoman Deborah Platt Majoras added: "Installations of secret software that create security risks are intrusive and unlawful. Consumers' computers belong to them, and companies must adequately disclose unexpected limitations on the customer use of their products so consumers can make informed decisions regarding whether to purchase and install that content."[42][43]

Copyright infringement

[edit]

Researchers found that Sony BMG and the makers of XCP also apparently infringed copyright by failing to adhere to the licensing requirements of various pieces of free and open-source software that was used in the program,[44][45] including the LAME MP3 encoder,[46] mpglib,[47] FAAC,[48] id3lib,[49] mpg123 and the VLC media player.[50]

In January 2006, the developers of LAME posted an open letter stating that they expected "appropriate action" by Sony BMG, but that the developers had no plans to investigate or take action over the apparent violation of LAME's source-code license.[51]

Company and press reports

[edit]

Russinovich's report was discussed on popular blogs almost immediately following its release.[52]

NPR was one of the first major news outlets to report on the scandal on November 4, 2005. Thomas Hesse, Sony BMG's president of global digital business, said: "Most people, I think, don't even know what a rootkit is, so why should they care about it?"[53]

In a November 7, 2005, article, vnunet.com summarized Russinovich's findings[54] and urged consumers to temporarily avoid purchasing Sony BMG music CDs. The following day, The Boston Globe classified the software as spyware, and Computer Associates' eTrust Security Management unit VP Steve Curry confirmed that the rootkit communicates personal information from consumers' computers (the CD being played and the user's IP address) to Sony BMG.[55] The methods used by the software to avoid detection were likened to those used by data thieves.

On November 8, 2005, Computer Associates classified Sony BMG's software as spyware and provided tools for its removal.[56] Russinovich said: "This is a step they should have taken immediately."[57]

The first virus to exploit Sony BMG's stealth technology to make malicious files invisible to both the user and antivirus programs surfaced on November 10, 2005.[58] One day later, Yahoo! News announced that Sony BMG had suspended further distribution of the controversial technology.[citation needed]

ZDNet News wrote: "The latest risk is from an uninstaller program distributed by SunnComm Technologies, a company that provides copy protection on other Sony BMG releases." The uninstall program obeys commands sent to it allowing others "to take control of PCs where the uninstaller has been used."[59]

On December 6, 2005, Sony BMG revealed that 5.7 million CDs spanning 27 titles were shipped with MediaMax 5 software. The company announced the availability of a new software patch to prevent a potential security breach in consumers' computers.

Sony BMG in Australia issued a press release indicating that no Sony BMG titles manufactured in Australia contained copy protection.[60]

On November 18, 2005, Sony BMG provided a "new and improved" removal tool to remove the rootkit component of XCP from affected Microsoft Windows computers.[citation needed] Legal and financial problems[edit] On November 15, 2005, vnunet.com announced[18] that Sony BMG was backing out of its copy-protection software, recalling unsold CDs from all stores and allowing consumers to exchange affected CDs for versions without the software. The Electronic Frontier Foundation compiled a partial list of CDs with XCP.[19] Sony BMG maintained that "there were no security risks associated with the anti-piracy technology" despite numerous virus and malware reports. On November 16, 2005, US-CERT, part of the United States Department of Homeland Security, issued an advisory on XCP DRM. It said that XCP uses rootkit technology to hide certain files from the user and that the technique is a security threat to users. They also said that one of the uninstallation options provided by Sony BMG introduces further vulnerabilities. US-CERT advised: "Do not install software from sources that you do not expect to contain software, such as an audio CD."[20] Sony BMG announced that it had instructed retailers to remove any unsold music discs containing the software from their shelves.[21] Internet-security expert Dan Kaminsky estimated that XCP was in use on more than 500,000 networks.[22] CDs with XCP technology can be identified by the letters "XCP" printed on the back cover of the jewel case for the CD according to SonyBMG's XCP FAQ.[23] On November 16, 2005, Reuters reported that Sony BMG would exchange affected CDs for new unprotected discs.[24] As a part of the swap program, consumers could mail their XCP-protected CDs to Sony BMG and receive an unprotected disc via return mail. On November 29, investigators for New York attorney general Eliot Spitzer found that, despite the recall of November 15, Sony BMG CDs with XCP were still for sale at some New York City music retail outlets. Spitzer said: "It is unacceptable that more than three weeks after this serious vulnerability was revealed, these same CDs are still on shelves, during the busiest shopping days of the year, [and] I strongly urge all retailers to heed the warnings issued about these products, pull them from distribution immediately, and ship them back to Sony."[25] The next day, Massachusetts attorney general Tom Reilly announced that Sony BMG CDs with XCP were still available in Boston despite the Sony BMG recall of November 15.[26] He advised consumers not to purchase the Sony BMG CDs with XCP and said that he was conducting an investigation of Sony BMG. Sony BMG's website offered US consumers a link to "Class Action Settlement Information Regarding XCP And MediaMax Content Protection"[27] with online claim filing and links to software updates and uninstallers. The deadline for submitting a claim was June 30, 2007. The website offered an explanation of the events as well as a list of all affected CDs.[28] On November 21, 2005, Texas attorney general Greg Abbott sued Sony BMG.[29] The suit was the first filed by a U.S. state and was also the first filed under the state's 2005 spyware law. It alleged that the company surreptitiously installed the spyware on millions of CDs. On December 21, 2005, Abbott added new allegations to the lawsuit,[30] claiming that MediaMax violated the state's spyware and deceptive trade practices laws because the MediaMax software would be installed on a computer even if the user declined the license agreement authorizing the action. Abbott stated: "We keep discovering additional methods Sony used to deceive Texas consumers who thought they were simply buying music", and "Thousands of Texans are now potential victims of this deceptive game Sony played with consumers for its own purposes." In addition to violations of the Consumer Protection Against Computer Spyware Act of 2005, which allowed for civil penalties of $100,000 for each violation of the law, the alleged violations added in the updated lawsuit carried maximum penalties of $20,000 per violation.[31][32] Sony was ordered to pay $750,000 in legal fees to Texas, accept customer returns of affected CDs, place a conspicuous detailed notice on its homepage, make "keyword buys" to alert consumers by advertising with Google, Yahoo! and MSN, pay up to $150 per damaged computer and agree to other remedies. Sony BMG also had to agree that it would not bring any claim that the legal settlement in any way constitutes the approval of the court.[33] New York and California class-action suits[edit] Class-action suits were filed against Sony BMG in New York and California.[34] On December 30, 2005, The New York Times reported that Sony BMG had reached a tentative settlement of the lawsuits, proposing two ways of compensating consumers who had purchased the affected CDs.[35] In Italy, ALCEI [it] (an association similar to EFF) also reported the rootkit to the Financial Police, asking for an investigation under various computer crime allegations, along with a technical analysis of the rootkit.[36][37] The U.S. Department of Justice made no comment on whether it would take any criminal action against Sony. However, Stewart Baker of the Department of Homeland Security publicly admonished Sony, stating, "it's your intellectual property—it's not your computer."[38] On November 21, the EFF announced that it was also pursuing a lawsuit over both XCP and the SunnComm MediaMax DRM technology. The EFF lawsuit also involved issues concerning the Sony BMG end-user license agreement. It was reported on December 24, 2005, that Florida attorney general Charlie Crist was investigating Sony BMG spyware.[39] On January 30, 2007, the U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC) announced a settlement with Sony BMG on charges that the CD copy protection had violated federal law[40]—Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act, 15 USC 45(a)—by engaging in unfair and deceptive business practices.[41] The settlement required Sony BMG to reimburse consumers up to $150 to repair damage that resulted directly from its attempts to remove the software installed without their consent.[40] The settlement also required them to provide clear and prominent disclosure on the packaging of future CDs of any limits on copying or restrictions on the use of playback devices, and the company was prohibited from installing content-protection software without obtaining consumers' authorization.[40] FTC chairwoman Deborah Platt Majoras added: "Installations of secret software that create security risks are intrusive and unlawful. Consumers' computers belong to them, and companies must adequately disclose unexpected limitations on the customer use of their products so consumers can make informed decisions regarding whether to purchase and install that content."[42][43] Copyright infringement[edit] Researchers found that Sony BMG and the makers of XCP also apparently infringed copyright by failing to adhere to the licensing requirements of various pieces of free and open-source software that was used in the program,[44][45] including the LAME MP3 encoder,[46] mpglib,[47] FAAC,[48] id3lib,[49] mpg123 and the VLC media player.[50] In January 2006, the developers of LAME posted an open letter stating that they expected "appropriate action" by Sony BMG, but that the developers had no plans to investigate or take action over the apparent violation of LAME's source-code license.[51] Company and press reports[edit] Russinovich's report was discussed on popular blogs almost immediately following its release.[52] NPR was one of the first major news outlets to report on the scandal on November 4, 2005. Thomas Hesse, Sony BMG's president of global digital business, said: "Most people, I think, don't even know what a rootkit is, so why should they care about it?"[53] In a November 7, 2005, article, vnunet.com summarized Russinovich's findings[54] and urged consumers to temporarily avoid purchasing Sony BMG music CDs. The following day, The Boston Globe classified the software as spyware, and Computer Associates' eTrust Security Management unit VP Steve Curry confirmed that the rootkit communicates personal information from consumers' computers (the CD being played and the user's IP address) to Sony BMG.[55] The methods used by the software to avoid detection were likened to those used by data thieves. On November 8, 2005, Computer Associates classified Sony BMG's software as spyware and provided tools for its removal.[56] Russinovich said: "This is a step they should have taken immediately."[57] The first virus to exploit Sony BMG's stealth technology to make malicious files invisible to both the user and antivirus programs surfaced on November 10, 2005.[58] One day later, Yahoo! News announced that Sony BMG had suspended further distribution of the controversial technology.[citation needed] ZDNet News wrote: "The latest risk is from an uninstaller program distributed by SunnComm Technologies, a company that provides copy protection on other Sony BMG releases." The uninstall program obeys commands sent to it allowing others "to take control of PCs where the uninstaller has been used."[59] On December 6, 2005, Sony BMG revealed that 5.7 million CDs spanning 27 titles were shipped with MediaMax 5 software. The company announced the availability of a new software patch to prevent a potential security breach in consumers' computers. blocks.html_en: In 2005, it was revealed that the implementation of copy protection measures on about 22 million CDs distributed by Sony BMG installed one of two pieces of software that provided a form of digital rights management (DRM) by modifying the operating system to interfere with CD copying. Neither program could easily be uninstalled, and they created vulnerabilities that were exploited by unrelated malware. One of the programs would install and "phone home" with reports on the user's private listening habits, even if the user refused its end-user license agreement (EULA), while the other was not mentioned in the EULA at all. Both programs contained code from several pieces of copylefted free software in an apparent infringement of copyright, and configured the operating system to hide the software's existence, leading to both programs being classified as rootkits.

blocks.html_en: [edit]

The two pieces of copy-protection software at issue in the 2005–2007 scandal were included on over 22 million CDs[7] marketed by Sony BMG, the record company formed by the 2004 merger of Sony and BMG's recorded music divisions. About two million of those CDs,[7] spanning 52 titles, contained First 4 Internet (F4I)'s Extended Copy Protection (XCP), which was installed on Microsoft Windows systems after the user accepted the EULA, which made no mention of the software. The remaining 20 million CDs,[7] spanning 50 titles,[8] contained SunnComm's MediaMax CD-3, which was installed on either Microsoft Windows or macOS systems after the user was presented with the EULA, regardless of whether the user accepted it. However, macOS prompted the user for confirmation when the software attempted to modify the OS, whereas Windows did not.

blocks.html_en: The scandal began on October 31, 2005, when Winternals researcher Mark Russinovich posted to his blog a detailed description and technical analysis of F4I's XCP software that he determined had been recently installed on his computer by a Sony BMG music CD. Russinovich compared the software to a rootkit because of its surreptitious installation and efforts to hide its existence. He noted that the EULA does not mention the software, and he charged that the software is illegitimate and that digital rights management had "gone too far".[9]

blocks.html_en: Sony BMG quickly released software to remove the rootkit component of XCP from affected Microsoft Windows computers,[15] but after Russinovich analyzed the utility, he reported in his blog that it only exacerbated the security problems and raised further concerns about privacy.[16] Russinovich noted that the removal program merely unmasked the hidden files installed by the rootkit but did not actually remove the rootkit. He also reported that it installed additional software that could not be uninstalled. In order to download the uninstaller, he found that it was necessary to provide an e-mail address (which the Sony BMG Privacy Policy implied was added to various bulk e-mail lists) and to install an ActiveX control containing backdoor methods (marked as "safe for scripting" and thus prone to exploits).[17] Microsoft later issued a killbit for the ActiveX control.

blocks.html_en: [edit]

On November 15, 2005, vnunet.com announced[18] that Sony BMG was backing out of its copy-protection software, recalling unsold CDs from all stores and allowing consumers to exchange affected CDs for versions without the software. The Electronic Frontier Foundation compiled a partial list of CDs with XCP.[19] Sony BMG maintained that "there were no security risks associated with the anti-piracy technology" despite numerous virus and malware reports. On November 16, 2005, US-CERT, part of the United States Department of Homeland Security, issued an advisory on XCP DRM. It said that XCP uses rootkit technology to hide certain files from the user and that the technique is a security threat to users. They also said that one of the uninstallation options provided by Sony BMG introduces further vulnerabilities. US-CERT advised: "Do not install software from sources that you do not expect to contain software, such as an audio CD."[20]

blocks.html_en: On December 21, 2005, Abbott added new allegations to the lawsuit,[30] claiming that MediaMax violated the state's spyware and deceptive trade practices laws because the MediaMax software would be installed on a computer even if the user declined the license agreement authorizing the action. blocks.html_en: On January 30, 2007, the U.S. Federal Trade Commission (FTC) announced a settlement with Sony BMG on charges that the CD copy protection had violated federal law[40]—Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act, 15 USC 45(a)—by engaging in unfair and deceptive business practices.[41] The settlement required Sony BMG to reimburse consumers up to $150 to repair damage that resulted directly from its attempts to remove the software installed without their consent.[40] The settlement also required them to provide clear and prominent disclosure on the packaging of future CDs of any limits on copying or restrictions on the use of playback devices, and the company was prohibited from installing content-protection software without obtaining consumers' authorization.[40] FTC chairwoman Deborah Platt Majoras added: "Installations of secret software that create security risks are intrusive and unlawful. Consumers' computers belong to them, and companies must adequately disclose unexpected limitations on the customer use of their products so consumers can make informed decisions regarding whether to purchase and install that content."[42][43]

blocks.html_en: • Revisiting Sony BMG Rootkit Scandal 10 years later

sentences.en: Revisiting Sony BMG Rootkit Scandal 10 years later
sentences.zh: 十年后重温索尼 BMG Rootkit 丑闻

content_html_zh:
2005 年，有消息称，索尼 BMG 分发的约 2200 万张 CD 上实施了复制保护措施，安装了两款软件之一，这些软件通过修改操作系统来干扰 CD 复制，提供某种形式的数字版权管理 (DRM)。 这两个程序都无法轻松卸载，并且它们创建了可被不相关恶意软件利用的漏洞。 即使用户拒绝其最终用户许可协议（EULA），其中一个程序也会安装并“打电话回家”，报告用户的私人收听习惯，而另一个程序在 EULA 中根本没有提及。 这两个程序都包含来自多个 Copyleft 自由软件的代码，明显侵犯了版权，并配置了操作系统来隐藏该软件的存在，导致这两个程序都被归类为 rootkit。

Sony BMG 最初否认 Rootkit 有害。 然后，它发布了其中一个程序的官方卸载程序，该卸载程序仅使该程序的文件可见，同时还安装了无法轻松删除的其他软件，收集了用户的电子邮件地址并引入了更多安全漏洞。

在 2005 年和 2006 年公众强烈抗议、政府调查和集体诉讼之后，索尼 BMG 通过与消费者达成和解、召回约 10% 的受影响 CD 以及于 2007 年初暂停 CD 复制保护工作，部分解决了这一丑闻。

2000 年 8 月，索尼影视娱乐公司美国高级副总裁史蒂夫·赫克勒 (Steve Heckler) 的声明预示了 2005 年末发生的事件。 赫克勒在美洲信息系统会议上告诉与会者：“该行业将采取一切必要措施来保护自己并保护其收入流...... 无论如何，它都不会失去收入来源...... 索尼将采取积极措施来阻止这种情况。 我们将开发超越个人用户的技术。 我们将在源头对 Napster 进行防火墙 – 我们将在您的有线电视公司处阻止它。 我们将在您的电话公司阻止它。 我们将在您的 ISP 处阻止它。 我们将在您的电脑上设置防火墙... 这些策略正在被积极推行，因为风险太大。”[1]

在欧洲，BMG 于 2001 年发行了娜塔莉·安博利亚 (Natalie Imbruglia) 的第二张专辑《White Lilies Island》，但没有警告标签表明该 CD 包含版权保护，引发了一场小丑闻。[2][3] CD 最终被更换。[2][3] BMG 和索尼均于 2001 年末在某些市场上发布了某些版本的受版权保护的版本，[4][5]，2002 年末的一份报告表明，在欧洲销售的所有 BMG CD 都将包含某种形式的版权保护。 [6]

复制保护软件

[edit]

2005-2007 年丑闻中涉及的两款版权保护软件包含在索尼 BMG 销售的超过 2200 万张 CD[7] 中，索尼 BMG 是一家由索尼和 BMG 唱片部门于 2004 年合并而成的唱片公司。 其中大约 200 万张 CD，[7] 涵盖 52 个标题，包含 First 4 Internet (F4I) 的扩展复制保护 (XCP)，在用户接受 EULA 后将其安装在 Microsoft Windows 系统上，但 EULA 中没有提及该软件。 其余 2000 万张 CD，[7] 涵盖 50 个标题，[8] 包含 SunnComm 的 MediaMax CD-3，在向用户提供 EULA 后，无论用户是否接受它，该 CD 都会安装在 Microsoft Windows 或 macOS 系统上。 然而，当软件尝试修改操作系统时，macOS 会提示用户确认，而 Windows 则不会。

该丑闻始于 2005 年 10 月 31 日，当时 Winternals 研究员 Mark Russinovich 在他的博客上发布了对 F4I XCP 软件的详细描述和技术分析，他确定该软件最近通过索尼 BMG 音乐 CD 安装在他的计算机上。 鲁西诺维奇将该软件比作 Rootkit，因为它的安装是秘密的，并努力隐藏其存在。 他指出，EULA 没有提及该软件，他指责该软件是非法的，并且数字版权管理“走得太远”。 [9]

反病毒公司 F-Secure 表示同意：“虽然该软件不是直接恶意的，但所使用的 Rootkit 隐藏技术与恶意软件所使用的隐藏技术完全相同。 DRM 软件会对所有检测 Rootkit 的 AV 软件造成许多类似的误报。 ... 因此，商业软件使用这些技术是非常不合适的。”[10]迫于舆论压力，赛门铁克[11]等反病毒厂商也在其产品中加入了对rootkit的检测，而微软则宣布将在其安全补丁中加入检测和清除功能。[12]

Russinovich 发现了 XCP 的许多问题：

  • 它会产生可被蠕虫或病毒等恶意软件利用的安全漏洞。
  • 无论是否正在播放受保护的 CD，它都会不断在后台运行并过度消耗系统资源，从而降低用户计算机的速度。
  • 它采用不安全的程序来启动和停止，这可能会导致系统崩溃。
  • 它没有卸载程序，并且安装方式不熟练，尝试卸载它可能会导致操作系统无法识别现有驱动器。

在 Russinovich 发表第一篇文章后不久，出现了一些利用 XCP 安全漏洞的木马和蠕虫。 [13]甚至有人利用该漏洞在网络游戏中进行作弊。 [14]

Sony BMG 迅速发布了软件，以从受影响的 Microsoft Windows 计算机中删除 XCP 的 rootkit 组件，[15] 但在 Russinovich 分析该实用程序后，他在博客中报告称，这只会加剧安全问题并引发对隐私的进一步担忧。 [16] Russinovich 指出，删除程序只是揭露了 Rootkit 安装的隐藏文件，但并未真正删除 Rootkit。 他还报告说，它安装了无法卸载的附加软件。 为了下载卸载程序，他发现有必要提供一个电子邮件地址（Sony BMG 隐私政策暗示已将其添加到各种批量电子邮件列表中）并安装包含后门方法的 ActiveX 控件（标记为“安全的脚本编写”，因此容易被利用）。 [17] Microsoft 后来为 ActiveX 控件发布了一个killbit。

2005 年 11 月 18 日，Sony BMG 提供了一个“新的和改进的”删除工具，用于从受影响的 Microsoft Windows 计算机中删除 XCP 的 rootkit 组件。 [需要引用]

法律和财务问题

[edit]

2005 年 11 月 15 日，vnunet.com 宣布[18] Sony BMG 将退出其复制保护软件，召回所有商店中未售出的 CD，并允许消费者将受影响的 CD 换成不带该软件的版本。 电子前沿基金会编制了带有 XCP 的部分 CD 列表。[19]尽管有大量病毒和恶意软件报告，索尼 BMG 仍坚称“不存在与反盗版技术相关的安全风险”。 2005 年 11 月 16 日，美国国土安全部下属的 US-CERT 发布了有关 XCP DRM 的咨询。 据称，XCP 使用 rootkit 技术向用户隐藏某些文件，该技术对用户构成安全威胁。 他们还表示，Sony BMG 提供的卸载选项之一引入了更多漏洞。 US-CERT 建议：“不要从您不希望包含软件的来源安装软件，例如音频 CD。”[20]

索尼 BMG 宣布已指示零售商将所有未售出的包含该软件的音乐光盘下架。 [21]互联网安全专家 Dan Kaminsky 估计 XCP 在超过 500,000 个网络上使用。 [22]

根据 SonyBMG 的 XCP 常见问题解答，采用 XCP 技术的 CD 可以通过 CD 珠宝盒后盖上印有的字母“XCP”来识别。 [23]

2005 年 11 月 16 日，路透社报道索尼 BMG 将用受影响的 CD 更换新的未受保护的光盘。 [24]作为交换计划的一部分，消费者可以将受 XCP 保护的 CD 邮寄给 Sony BMG，并通过回邮收到未受保护的光盘。

11 月 29 日，纽约总检察长艾略特·斯皮策 (Eliot Spitzer) 的调查人员发现，尽管 11 月 15 日进行了召回，但带有 XCP 的索尼 BMG CD 仍在纽约市的一些音乐零售店出售。 斯皮策说：“在这一严重漏洞被揭露三周多后，在一年中最繁忙的购物日，这些相同的 CD 仍在货架上，这是不可接受的，[并且]我强烈敦促所有零售商注意有关这些产品的警告，立即将其从分销中撤回，并将其运回索尼。”[25]

第二天，马萨诸塞州总检察长汤姆·赖利 (Tom Reilly) 宣布，尽管索尼 BMG 于 11 月 15 日召回，但带 XCP 的索尼 BMG CD 在波士顿仍然有售。 [26]他建议消费者不要购买带有XCP的索尼BMG CD，并表示他正在对索尼BMG进行调查。

Sony BMG 的网站为美国消费者提供了“有关 XCP 和 MediaMax 内容保护的集体诉讼和解信息”[27] 的链接，其中包含在线索赔申请以及软件更新和卸载程序的链接。 提交索赔的截止日期是2007年6月30日。 该网站提供了对事件的解释以及所有受影响 CD 的列表。 [28]

2005年11月21日，得克萨斯州总检察长格雷格·阿博特起诉索尼BMG。 [29]该诉讼是美国各州首次提起的诉讼，也是根据该州 2005 年间谍软件法提起的首次诉讼。 据称该公司秘密地将间谍软件安装在数百万张 CD 上。

2005 年 12 月 21 日，雅培在诉讼中添加了新的指控，[30] 声称 MediaMax 违反了该州的间谍软件和欺骗性贸易行为法，因为即使用户拒绝授权该行动的许可协议，MediaMax 软件也会安装在计算机上。 阿博特表示：“我们不断发现索尼用来欺骗德克萨斯州消费者的其他方法，他们认为他们只是购买音乐”，并且“成千上万的德克萨斯人现在成为索尼为了自己的目的而与消费者玩的欺骗游戏的潜在受害者。” 除了违反 2005 年《消费者保护计算机间谍软件法案》（该法案允许每次违法行为处以 100,000 美元的民事处罚）外，更新后的诉讼中添加的涉嫌违法行为每次违法行为的最高处罚为 20,000 美元。[31][32]索尼被责令向德克萨斯州支付 75 万美元的法律费用，接受客户退回受影响的 CD，在其主页上放置明显的详细通知，通过在 Google、Yahoo! 上做广告进行“关键字购买”以提醒消费者。 和 MSN，为每台损坏的计算机支付最多 150 美元的费用，并同意其他补救措施。 索尼 BMG 还必须同意，它不会提出任何主张，认为法律和解以任何方式构成法院的批准。 [33]

纽约和加州集体诉讼

[edit]

在纽约和加利福尼亚州对索尼 BMG 提起了集体诉讼。 [34]

2005年12月30日，《纽约时报》报道称，索尼BMG已就诉讼达成初步和解，提出了两种补偿购买受影响CD的消费者的方法。 [35]

在意大利，ALCEI [it]（类似于 EFF 的协会）也向金融警察局报告了该 Rootkit，要求对各种计算机犯罪指控进行调查，并对 Rootkit 进行技术分析。[36][37]

美国司法部没有评论是否会对索尼采取任何刑事行动。 然而，国土安全部的斯图尔特·贝克公开警告索尼，称“这是你的知识产权——不是你的计算机。”[38]

11 月 21 日，EFF 宣布正在就 XCP 和 SunnComm MediaMax DRM 技术提起诉讼。 EFF 诉讼还涉及索尼 BMG 最终用户许可协议的问题。

据2005年12月24日报道，佛罗里达州总检察长查理·克里斯特正在调查索尼BMG间谍软件。 [39]

2007 年 1 月 30 日，美国联邦贸易委员会 (FTC) 宣布与索尼 BMG 达成和解，指控其 CD 复制保护违反了联邦法律[40]——《联邦贸易委员会法》第 5(a) 条，15 USC 45(a)——从事不公平和欺骗性的商业行为。[41]和解协议要求索尼 BMG 向消费者赔偿高达 150 美元的损失，以修复因试图删除未经消费者同意而安装的软件而直接造成的损坏。 [40]和解还要求他们在未来 CD 的包装上明确、显着地披露任何复制限制或播放设备使用限制，并且禁止该公司在未获得消费者授权的情况下安装内容保护软件。 [40]联邦贸易委员会主席黛博拉·普拉特·马约拉斯补充道：“安装造成安全风险的秘密软件是侵入性的和非法的。 消费者的计算机属于他们，公司必须充分披露客户使用其产品的意外限制，以便消费者能够就是否购买和安装该内容做出明智的决定。”[42][43]

侵犯版权

[edit]

研究人员发现，索尼 BMG 和 XCP 的制造商也明显侵犯了版权，因为他们未能遵守该程序中使用的各种免费和开源软件的许可要求，[44][45]，包括 LAME MP3 编码器、[46] mpglib、[47] FAAC、[48] id3lib、[49] mpg123 和 VLC 媒体播放器。 [50]

2006 年 1 月，LAME 的开发人员发表了一封公开信，表示他们期望 Sony BMG 采取“适当的行动”，但开发人员没有计划对明显违反 LAME 源代码许可证的行为进行调查或采取行动。 [51]

公司及新闻报道

[edit]

Russinovich 的报告发布后几乎立即在热门博客上进行了讨论。[52]

NPR 是 2005 年 11 月 4 日最早报道这一丑闻的主要新闻媒体之一。 索尼 BMG 全球数字业务总裁 Thomas Hesse 表示：“我认为，大多数人甚至不知道 rootkit 是什么，所以他们为什么要关心它呢？”[53]

在 2005 年 11 月 7 日的一篇文章中，vnunet.com 总结了 Russinovich 的发现[54]，并敦促消费者暂时避免购买索尼 BMG 音乐 CD。 第二天，《波士顿环球报》将该软件归类为间谍软件，Computer Associates 的 eTrust 安全管理部门副总裁 Steve Curry 确认该 rootkit 将消费者计算机上的个人信息（正在播放的 CD 和用户的 IP 地址）传送给 Sony BMG。 [55]该软件用来避免检测的方法类似于数据窃贼所使用的方法。

2005 年 11 月 8 日，Computer Associates 将 Sony BMG 的软件归类为间谍软件，并提供了删除该软件的工具。 [56]鲁西诺维奇说：“这是他们应该立即采取的步骤。”[57]

第一个利用 Sony BMG 隐形技术使恶意文件对用户和防病毒程序均不可见的病毒于 2005 年 11 月 10 日出现。 [58]一天后，雅虎！ 新闻宣布索尼 BMG 已暂停进一步分发这项有争议的技术。[需要引用]

ZDNet News 写道：“最新的风险来自 SunnComm Technologies 分发的卸载程序，该公司为其他索尼 BMG 版本提供复制保护。” 卸载程序服从发送给它的命令，允许其他人“控制使用卸载程序的电脑。”[59]

2005 年 12 月 6 日，Sony BMG 透露，涵盖 27 个标题的 570 万张 CD 均配有 MediaMax 5 软件。 该公司宣布推出新的软件补丁，以防止消费者计算机中潜在的安全漏洞。

澳大利亚索尼 BMG 发布新闻稿称，澳大利亚制造的索尼 BMG 游戏均不包含版权保护。 [60]
